content.p: On 20 November 1991, two days after the Croatian town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People's Army and Serb forces, more than 200 Croats and other non-Serbs were taken out of the town's hospital. By the end of that day, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia later found, 194 of them had been killed near the Ovčara farm. It was among the worst single atrocities of the war in Croatia.

The case produced two very different kinds of justice. In The Hague, two army officers were convicted of aiding and abetting crimes against the prisoners, and a third was acquitted. In Belgrade, a domestic court tried the men who did the killing. The tribunal's judges found that neither of the two convicted officers had ordered the murders, and several dozen victims have still not been found.

According to the ICTY, the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) laid siege to Vukovar in late August 1991. The siege lasted until 18 November, when the city fell to Serb forces. The tribunal's indictment said that JNA shelling had largely destroyed the city and killed hundreds of people before it fell. It added that after the occupation hundreds more non-Serbs were killed, and that the great majority of the remaining non-Serb population was expelled within days.

In the siege's final days, several hundred people sheltered at the hospital, hoping for an evacuation that observers from abroad would witness. The commander of the Serb forces in the Vukovar area was Colonel Mile Mrkšić, who led the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade and Operational Group South. Under him was Major Veselin Šljivančanin, the security officer of both formations. A third officer, Captain Miroslav Radić, commanded an infantry company of the brigade's 1st Battalion.

The tribunal's judges found that on Mrkšić's orders, given on 19 November and carried out by Šljivančanin, prisoners of war were taken from the hospital on the morning of 20 November and eventually reached Ovčara. The detainees included wounded patients, hospital staff, soldiers who had defended the city, Croatian political activists and other civilians, according to the 1995 indictment announcement. The Trial Chamber was satisfied that Mrkšić first intended to send the prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica, among other things so that they could later be exchanged for Serb prisoners held by Croatia, which is what had happened to other prisoners in the preceding days.

That plan changed during the morning, the judges found. The prisoners sat in buses at the JNA barracks, then were put in a hangar at Ovčara. At each stop JNA military police still guarded them, though not effectively. At the barracks and at Ovčara, Serb Territorial Defence (TO) and paramilitary men beat and humiliated them, and the Trial Chamber found that these abuses were reported to Mrkšić by several officers.

The Humanitarian Law Center, a Serbian human rights organisation, says that members of the Vukovar TO and a paramilitary unit called Leva Supoderica beat, abused and humiliated the detainees at Ovčara while JNA military police were present. Late in the day, the tribunal found, Mrkšić ordered the military police guarding the prisoners to leave. Balkan Investigative Reporting Network says that in the evening paramilitaries led the captives out of the storage building in groups of 20, then executed and buried them. The indictment gave the group size as 10 to 20, and the Humanitarian Law Center says the groups were taken to the Grabovo site and shot in front of a mass grave that had been dug in advance. The indictment said the bodies were buried by bulldozer at the same place.

The dead included two women and three minors, the Humanitarian Law Center says. Ružica Markobašić was 32 and heavily pregnant; Janja Podhorski was 60; the three minors were Dragutin Balog (17), Igor Kačić (16) and Tomislav Baumgertner (17). Those identified from the grave ranged in age from 16 to 77, according to the same organisation in its 2010 account.

Sources do not agree on how many people were taken from the hospital or how many died. The 1995 ICTY announcement named 261 men. In 2007 the tribunal's press office spoke of about 260 non-Serb individuals. The later case information sheet said that, according to the indictment, at least 264 captives were killed, and the Balkan network database puts the number seized at about 250. The Humanitarian Law Center, in 2024, spoke of 265 Croatian civilians and prisoners of war killed.

The judges used a more cautious figure. They said the exhumations and autopsies established the 194 named victims, and stressed that more than 200 people may have died at Ovčara that day, of whom 194 have been identified. The Humanitarian Law Center says 200 bodies were exhumed from the grave and 193 identified. The Balkan network database says 200 sets of remains and 192 identified. Another count in the Humanitarian Law Center's 2010 account is 194 identified by July 2006. These differences are in the sources and no page opened here reconciles them.

According to the Balkan network database, UN officials first identified the Ovčara site in December 1992 but were refused permission to investigate. A second UN visit in 1993 met the same refusal from the rebel Croatian Serb authorities, who held the area until the war ended. The International Commission on Missing Persons, citing Physicians for Human Rights, says that organisation discovered the mass grave in October 1992. The two accounts differ on who found it and when.

After the Croatian Serb administration was ousted, exhumation began. The Commission says Physicians for Human Rights began exhuming remains on 1 September 1996 on behalf of the ICTY, with Croatian observers present, and that by 1 October the grave had yielded 200 sets of remains. It was the largest mass grave from 1991 and 1992. The database describes the pit as ten metres long, seven wide and one and a half to two metres deep. The Humanitarian Law Center's 2024 statement adds that the remains of 17 victims were found in nearby graves.

The ICTY announced the first indictment against Mrkšić, Radić and Šljivančanin on 30 October 1995; the judge confirmed it on 7 November. It charged them with the mass killing at Ovčara of about 260 captive non-Serb men and alleged that they were criminally responsible both individually and as commanders. Rule 61 hearings, held from 20 to 28 March 1996, led the Trial Chamber to confirm the indictment and issue international arrest warrants. The chamber attributed the failure to arrest the three men to the refusal of Belgrade, then the capital of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to co-operate, and the tribunal's president reported this to the UN Security Council.

Slavko Dokmanović, vice president of the Vukovar municipality, was added to the indictment in April 1996. He pleaded not guilty and died in custody on 29 June 1998, and the proceedings against him were ended. Mrkšić surrendered on 15 May 2002. Radić was transferred to the tribunal on 17 May 2003, and Šljivančanin was arrested by the Serbian authorities on 13 June 2003 and transferred on 1 July 2003.
The trial opened on 11 October 2005 and lasted 189 trial days. It heard 62 prosecution witnesses and 36 for the defence. On 27 September 2007 the Trial Chamber delivered its judgement.

The Trial Chamber dismissed all charges of crimes against humanity. It found the people killed at Ovčara had been "specifically identified and selected because of their known, or believed, involvement in the Croatian forces in Vukovar", and that the Serb forces who mistreated and murdered them "acted on the understanding that the victims were prisoners of war, not civilians." It found no evidence of a joint criminal enterprise among the three accused. The perpetrators of the murders, torture and beatings, it said, were members of the Serb Territorial Defence led by Miroljub Vujović, many from the Vukovar area, together with paramilitaries. It found that neither Mrkšić nor Šljivančanin had ordered them.

Mrkšić was convicted of aiding and abetting murder, torture and cruel treatment. The judges found that he knew the TO and paramilitary forces were at Ovčara and knew the danger they posed to the prisoners, yet withdrew the JNA guards, apparently in response to pressure from the local Serb government. He was sentenced to 20 years. Šljivančanin was convicted of aiding and abetting torture, because he failed to secure adequate guards at Ovčara or to see that the guards present acted to stop the beatings. He received five years. Radić was acquitted of all charges. The judges found that he was at the hospital on 19 and 20 November, and that soldiers under his command provided its initial security, but not that he took part in separating the people in front of the hospital, or that he knew soldiers under his command had committed crimes at Ovčara. He was released at once.

Both sides appealed. On 5 May 2009 the Appeals Chamber dismissed all of Mrkšić's eleven grounds and all of Šljivančanin's six, and kept Mrkšić's 20 years. It accepted the prosecution's case on one point: Šljivančanin, it held, formed the knowledge needed for aiding and abetting murder once he learned that night of the order to withdraw the troops, because the only reasonable inference was that he then realised the prisoners would likely be killed. His sentence was raised to 17 years. After a review judgement on 8 December 2010 it was cut to ten years, and he was granted early release on 5 July 2011. Mrkšić was transferred to Portugal to serve the rest of his sentence on 16 August 2012 and died on 16 August 2015, according to the tribunal's information sheet.

The residual mechanism that now maintains the tribunal's records says two people were acquitted of Ovčara crimes, Radić and the Serbian Radical Party leader Vojislav Šešelj, and that three died before verdict: Slobodan Milošević, Dokmanović and the Croatian Serb leader Goran Hadžić.

A second set of trials took place before the War Crimes Trial Chamber of the Belgrade District Court. The Humanitarian Law Center's 2010 account lists sentences of 20 years for six men, 15 for two, 13 for one, 11 for one woman, 6 for one, and 5 for two more, and acquittals for five. Its 2024 statement describes a trial lasting 14 years, in which only the direct perpetrators were prosecuted. It says 24 members of the Vukovar TO and the Leva Supoderica unit were indicted, 11 were convicted with final sentences of two to twenty years, nine were acquitted, two became cooperating witnesses and two died during the trial. The Balkan network database counts ten convicted in Serbia, and twelve in total, with the two ICTY convictions, serving 161 years between them. The sources differ on the Serbian numbers.

After the final verdict in Serbia, the Humanitarian Law Center filed compensation suits for victims' families. Eleven cases concluded in the plaintiffs' favour, which the organisation describes as Serbia's formal acknowledgment of its responsibility for the crime.

A monument to the victims was installed at the grave site in December 1998, with 200 bushes planted, one for each victim. The storage building where the prisoners were held became the Memorial Home Ovčara, which opened in 2006. The farm had belonged to a state agricultural company that was privatised in 2010; its land is now part of the Memorial Centre of the Homeland War.

The International Commission on Missing Persons says that 61 people last seen after the hospital was taken are still missing, and that Croatia's missing persons directorate reports that Serbia has returned only part of the documentation the JNA seized from the hospital, including patient protocols. The Humanitarian Law Center counted 48 victims still missing in 2024. It calls for the JNA archives to be opened and for members of the units involved to give what information they have.

The same statement criticises what it calls the social and political rehabilitation in Serbia of Šljivančanin, who has published books, appeared as an analyst and served on the main board of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party. The Trial Chamber had found that neither Mrkšić nor Šljivančanin ordered the murders, torture and beatings, and it named the Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces as the perpetrators.
